content.title: About
content.content: Beef and broccoli is a popular Asian‑inspired dish featuring tender strips of beef quickly stir‑fried with a soy‑based sauce, ginger, garlic, and crisp broccoli florets. The meal is rich in protein, B‑vitamins, and fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish became popular in the United States in the 1970s as an adaptation of Chinese beef‑broccoli stir‑fry.
Beef is traditionally sliced thinly across the grain to keep it tender.
Broccoli is technically a “flower” and is packed with vitamin C and K.
A touch of cornstarch in the sauce gives it a glossy, slightly thickened texture.
It is commonly served over rice or noodles, making it a complete meal.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef supplies B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Fiber and antioxidants from broccoli
items.content: Broccoli delivers vitamin C, K, folate, and sulforaphane, a compound with anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Beef is a good source of iron and zinc, important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Low carbohydrate profile
items.content: When served without large portions of rice or noodles, the dish fits well into low‑carb eating plans.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Choosing lean cuts (e.g., sirloin, tenderloin) reduces saturated fat intake.

items.title: Sodium in the sauce
items.content: Soy sauce can add a lot of salt; opt for low‑sodium versions or use less.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy should substitute tamari or coconut aminos.

items.title: Potential bacterial contamination
items.content: Cook beef to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C (145 °F) to ensure safety.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice beef thinly, marinate in soy sauce, ginger, and garlic for 15‑20 minutes. Stir‑fry quickly over high heat, add broccoli and a splash of water or broth, then pour in the sauce thickened with cornstarch. Serve hot over rice or noodles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Raw beef keeps in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days; cooked beef and broccoli can be stored in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Freeze separate portions of beef and broccoli in freezer‑safe bags for up to 3 months.

chicken-or-turkey-and-rice-with-mushroom.title: Chicken or turkey and rice with mushroom sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of boiled rice, tender chicken or turkey meat, and a flavorful mushroom sauce. Mushrooms (usually button mushrooms) are sautéed with onion and garlic, then simmered with broth and cream to create a rich, creamy sauce that coats the meat and rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mushroom sauce is often finished with cream, giving the dish a silky texture.
Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein, while rice supplies complex carbohydrates for sustained energy.
In traditional Russian cuisine this meal is often served on festive occasions, combining simplicity with elegance.
Mushrooms are rich in B‑vitamins and minerals such as selenium and potassium.
Adding dried herbs like thyme, rosemary, or oregano can enhance the flavor profile.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey contain all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Energy‑providing carbs
items.content: Rice offers complex carbohydrates that release glucose slowly, helping maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms provide vitamins B2, B3 and B5, important for metabolic processes.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish supplies iron, zinc and selenium, which support immune function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When lean poultry cuts and moderate amounts of cream are used, the meal remains relatively heart‑friendly.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Using ready‑made broths or soy sauce can raise the sodium level of the sauce.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cream and butter increase the calorie count; portion control is advisable.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: Improperly stored chicken or turkey can harbor salmonella or campylobacter.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, placing rice on a plate, topping with chicken or turkey pieces, and drizzling the mushroom sauce over everything. Garnish with fresh herbs (parsley, dill) and a squeeze of lemon for brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. When reheating, add a splash of broth or milk to prevent the sauce from becoming too thick.

chicken-or-turkey-stuffing-and-vegetable.title: Chicken or turkey with stuffing and vegetables without carrots, broccoli, and dark green leafy, no sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of roasted chicken or turkey breast fillet, stuffed with a mixture of whole grains, mushrooms and aromatic herbs, accompanied by vegetables such as zucchini, sweet pepper and cauliflower. It is prepared without carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy vegetables and without sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are excellent sources of lean protein.
The stuffing often includes whole grains like quinoa or bulgur, boosting the nutritional value.
Absence of sauce makes the dish lighter and lets the natural flavors of meat and vegetables shine.
Cauliflower used in the side dish is rich in vitamin C and fiber.
Traditionally the dish is baked at 180‑200 °C until a golden crust forms.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: White meat contains less saturated fat than red meat, supporting heart health.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables and grains
items.content: The side and stuffing deliver dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Cauliflower and sweet pepper provide vitamin C and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Overcooking
items.content: Overbaking can make the meat dry and reduce protein digestibility.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If using pre‑made seasonings, watch the salt level to avoid excess sodium intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw poultry can harbor salmonella; ensure the meat reaches an internal temperature of 74 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, slicing the fillet into portions. A squeeze of fresh lemon juice or a drizzle of herb‑infused olive oil adds extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave until the internal temperature reaches 74 °C.

classic-mixed-vegetables-frozen-cooked-w.title: Classic mixed vegetables, frozen, cooked with oil

content.title: About
content.content: The classic frozen mixed vegetables cooked in vegetable oil contain carrots, peas, corn, beans and other vegetables. They heat quickly, retain colour, flavour and nutrients, making them a convenient side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetables are flash‑frozen right after harvest, preserving most of their vitamins.
Cooking in oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A and K.
The mix is commonly used in Asian and Mediterranean cuisines.
Rapid freezing prevents large ice crystals, keeping the texture intact.
The product has a long shelf life without added preservatives.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A and C
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision and immunity, while vitamin C acts as an antioxidant protecting cells.

items.title: Source of dietary fibre
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: Vegetables contribute a modest amount of protein, useful when combined with other foods.

items.title: Improved uptake of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Cooking in oil increases the bioavailability of vitamins A and K.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oil
items.content: Some individuals may react to the oil used in processing.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain batches may contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Loss of crisp texture over time
items.content: After thawing, the vegetables can become softer, affecting texture preferences.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the vegetables in a pan, microwave, or steamer. Add them to soups, stews, pasta, rice dishes, or serve as a side with meat or fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once opened, use within 3–4 months. Do not thaw and refreeze the product.

content.title: About
content.content: Fish sauce is a liquid seasoning made by fermenting fish (usually anchovies) with salt. It is a staple in Southeast Asian cuisines, providing a distinctive salty‑umami flavor and aroma to dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Thai fish sauce, called “nam pla,” has been produced for over 200 years.
Vietnamese fish sauce (“nuoc mam”) is often aged up to two years to deepen its flavor.
Fermentation releases amino acids, especially glutamate, which is responsible for the umami taste.
Fish sauce can be light (milder) or dark (more intense) depending on the length of aging.
In some countries the sauce is considered a national product and enjoys protected geographical status.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Fermentation retains a portion of fish protein, which is easily digestible.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Fish sauce provides vitamin B12, essential for nerve function and blood formation.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fermented foods may promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many sauces, fish sauce contains virtually no fat.

items.title: Enhances flavor without extra salt
items.content: Because of its strong umami profile, a small amount can replace a larger quantity of salt in recipes.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Fish sauce is very salty; people with hypertension should limit its use.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to seafood may experience reactions after consuming the sauce.

items.title: Histamine levels
items.content: Fermented products can contain histamine, which may trigger headaches in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Product quality
items.content: Low‑quality sauces may contain additives, artificial flavors, and preservatives.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add fish sauce to marinades, sauces, soups, salads, and stir‑fries. A few drops can boost the flavor of soy sauce, curry pastes, or tomato sauces. It is often combined with lime, garlic, and sugar to create classic Asian dressings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fish sauce in a tightly sealed bottle in the refrigerator after opening. Properly stored, it retains its flavor for up to a year. Discard if it becomes cloudy, changes color, or develops an off smell.

content.title: About
content.content: French or Catalina Dressing is a flavorful sauce made from mayonnaise, tomato sauce, vinegar, sugar and spices. It combines sweet‑sour notes with a mild tang, making it popular for salads, seafood, and chicken dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dressing was first created in the United States in the mid‑20th century and quickly became a staple of California cuisine.
The name “Catalina” comes from Catalina Island, where the sauce was often served in seaside restaurants.
There are several recipe variations: some add mustard, others include anchovies for extra depth.
It is frequently used as a grill marinade as well as in sandwiches and wraps.
In Russia the sauce is often called “French dressing,” although the original recipe is American.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: The tomato component provides vitamin A, important for vision and immune function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vinegar and tomatoes add vitamin C, an antioxidant that supports cell protection.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: The mayonnaise base supplies monounsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart‑healthy diet when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Vinegar may aid digestion and improve nutrient absorption.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and spices are rich in antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A mayonnaise‑based dressing is calorie‑dense; excessive intake can contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise contains eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar and salt levels
items.content: The recipe includes sugar and salt, which may be undesirable for low‑sodium or low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Preservatives in commercial versions
items.content: Store‑bought dressings may contain artificial preservatives and flavorings that some people prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: French or Catalina Dressing works well as a salad dressing, a dip for seafood or chicken, and as a spread in sandwiches and wraps. It can also be mixed into marinades for meat or used as a dip for vegetable sticks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dressing refrigerated at 1 °C–4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, it is usually good for 1–2 weeks. Discard if the smell, color, or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn is made from corn kernels that explode when heated, creating light, airy pieces. This plain, light ready‑to‑eat popcorn contains no additives, flavorings, or salt, making it a low‑calorie snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn has been known since ancient times; archaeologists have found popcorn remnants in Mayan tombs.
Each kernel holds about 14 % water; when heated, the water turns to steam and forces the kernel to pop.
There are over 300 varieties of corn, but only a few are suitable for popcorn.
Popcorn is one of the most popular cinema snacks worldwide.
Light popcorn is often sold in single‑serve bags, which helps with portion control.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Light popcorn provides roughly 350 kcal per 100 g, making it a good alternative to more calorie‑dense snacks.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Popcorn is a source of dietary fiber, supporting digestive health and promoting satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols in popcorn help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Popcorn is naturally gluten‑free, suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Unlike oil‑popped varieties, light popcorn contains virtually no added fats.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn, experiencing skin rashes, swelling, or breathing difficulties.

items.title: Mycotoxin risk if stored improperly
items.content: When kept in humid conditions, popcorn can develop mold and produce mycotoxins; store it in a dry place.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: Small popcorn pieces can pose a choking risk for children under 4 years old.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Popcorn has a high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy popcorn as a stand‑alone snack, add it to salads, use it as a crunchy base for sweet desserts (with honey or berries), or incorporate it into recipes that call for a light, crispy element.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep popcorn in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, refrigerate to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crunch.
